status_summary: Major monopolization cases continued after 2025-01-20 with mixed court results. In the Google search case the court ordered data sharing and a ban on exclusive distribution deals on 2025-09-02 but refused to require divestiture of Chrome or Android, and in July 2026 DOJ and states asked the D.C. Circuit for harsher remedies; in the ad tech case the court on 2026-09-02 rejected divestiture of AdX and accepted most behavioral measures; the court ruled for Meta in the FTC's case on 2025-11-18, and the FTC appealed. Executive Order 14337 (signed 2025-08-13) revoked the 2021 competition order. On the crony-capitalism half, a judge approved the HPE and Juniper merger settlement on 2026-08-12 while finding Justice Department and HPE violations of Tunney Act transparency rules, after lobbying that reportedly reached department leadership, which runs against the recommendation; no distinct crackdown on corporate political influence was found.

timeline.event: President signs Executive Order 14337 (published 2025-08-19) revoking Executive Order 14036 of 2021, Promoting Competition in the American Economy; the order states no reasons and does not impair agencies' legal authority.

The court in United States v. Google (search) orders Google to share certain search index and user interaction data with qualified competitors and bars exclusive search distribution deals, while rejecting the government's request to force divestiture of Chrome and Android.

Judge Boasberg rules in FTC v. Meta that the FTC did not prove Meta holds monopoly power, pointing to competition from TikTok and YouTube; the FTC says it is disappointed and it later confirmed an appeal (2026-01-20 report).
An FTC spokesperson confirms the Commission will appeal the Meta ruling to the D.C. Circuit.

DOJ and plaintiff states file a response and cross-appeal brief in the D.C. Circuit in the Google search case, arguing the district court erred in rejecting a ban on Google's search-related payments to distributors.

Judge Casey Pitts approves the settlement allowing HPE to acquire Juniper Networks, saying the deal may lessen competition but the court lacks independent power to prevent it, and finding that HPE and the Justice Department violated Tunney Act disclosure rules without barring approval; reports describe HPE's appeal to department leadership with help from lobbyists and the later removal of two senior antitrust officials.

Judge Brinkema (E.D. Va., United States v. Google LLC, No. 1:23-cv-00108) issues a Memorandum Opinion (ECF 1858, held under seal for 14 days for redaction requests) and an Order (ECF 1857) rejecting divestiture of Google's AdX ad exchange, open-sourcing of DoubleClick for Publishers final auction logic and contingent divestiture of the rest of DFP, and accepting most proposed behavioral remedies as modified; the Order directs the parties to file one jointly proposed Final Judgment within 30 days.

title: Pair pro-growth policy with antitrust enforcement and curbs on crony capitalism
uncertainties: The Foreword sets no standard for what counts as a crackdown on crony capitalism, so the second half is judged only from the HPE and Juniper episode, which is read through trade-press reports of a court ruling, not the opinion; its date is inferred (2026-08-12) from a Daily Journal report of 2026-08-13 that said late Wednesday. The Google search remedies ruling was read through a law-firm note, not the opinion; the ad tech ruling was read on the court's Order (ECF 1857) and Memorandum Opinion (ECF 1858), both copies hosted by Courthouse News that carry the court's caption and docket header, and the law-firm note states the search remedies ruling issued on 2025-09-02. The Google, Meta and HPE matters, and the Amazon and Apple cases (not examined here), mostly began before 2025-01-20; continuing them is counted as alignment only in part. The Bloomberg page was opened in review and confirms the FTC appeal but shows no date; the 2026-01-20 date comes from its URL and from c30-04. The FTC Amazon Prime consumer-protection settlement and Apple and Live Nation antitrust cases were not checked. The Meta ruling's impeachment reference in the FTC statement was not verified. Related record c30-04 carries more FTC detail. Update 2026-10-27: proposed final judgments in the ad tech case were reported filed in early October (AdExchanger, ppc.land) but entry of a final judgment was not found, and the sealed opinion's term and monitor details were taken from trade press only. The HPE and Juniper order (N.D. Cal. No. 25-cv-00951-PCP, 2026-08-12) was read by the researcher as a PDF hosted by the California Attorney General, an intervening state and so a lead-only host, and is not cited; as a lead it indicates entry of the final judgment under the Tunney Act and findings of incomplete disclosure by HPE and Juniper and of an incomplete competitive impact statement by the United States. Review of 2026-10-27: a search found no report of entry of a final judgment in the ad tech case; the Memorandum Opinion's ruling on the monitor's term was not reached in the excerpt read. The HPE and Juniper date and findings still rest on news reports; the court's own order was not found on a qualifying host.
